scenes.narration: Meet Hiro. He makes small, precise metal parts in a workshop in a mountain town in Japan, parts that end up inside cars and machines all over the world. For a long time now, the same paper sign has hung in his window. Help wanted. Nobody calls. Hiro isn't unlucky. His whole country is running out of workers. And yet, a short drive from towns like his, Japan builds almost four in every ten industrial robots made on Earth. So could the world's oldest big country turn its biggest problem into its biggest advantage?

Hoshimachi isn't a real town, but towns like it are all over Japan. The train comes less often. More shops keep their shutters down. Hiro's apprentice left for the city years ago, and his stool still sits by the lathe. The strange thing is, Hiro's customers aren't leaving. They want more parts than ever. What's missing is hands.

Let me draw what happened. This bar is everyone of working age in Japan, at the peak, a generation ago. This bar is today. Since that peak, Japan has lost about thirteen and a half million working-age people. That's almost as many people as live in all of Tokyo. Picture every office and every train in Tokyo, empty. That's the size of the hole.

keyframes.cue: That's the size of the hole
keyframes.label: actions[2].at.cue

scenes.narration: And it isn't slowing down. The government's own population researchers project that, within the lifetime of today's children, Japan will have only about half the working-age people it had at the peak. Think of a rush-hour train platform, where you can barely move. Now take away every other person.

You can feel it in the job market. Month after month, Japan has had more open jobs than people looking for work. Hiro is competing for workers with the convenience store, the nursing home and the delivery company. And they're all losing too.

Take the trucks that carry Hiro's parts. Japan capped truck drivers' overtime to protect their health. Good for the drivers. But fewer drivers, working fewer hours, move fewer boxes. The government warns that, if nothing changes, by the end of the decade Japan could be short of trucks for about a third of its cargo.

Then there's Hiro's mother. She lives in a care home down the road. It needs more caregivers every year, because more people grow old and fewer young people arrive to help. The health ministry's own estimate is that Japan will need hundreds of thousands more caregivers in the years ahead.
Even Hiro's granddaughter, Aoi, moved away. She writes software in Tokyo now. Hiro is proud of her. He still needs someone to run the lathe.

So far, this sounds like the story everyone tells about Japan. Old, shrinking, stuck. But here's the twist. The same kind of shortage that is emptying Hoshimachi helped create one of Japan's greatest industries.

Go back to nineteen sixty-nine. Japan's economy was booming and factories couldn't hire fast enough. Kawasaki, a heavy-industry company, began building the first industrial robot made in Japan, under an American license. Carmakers hungry for workers were among the first buyers.

Today, the International Federation of Robotics calls Japan the world's predominant robot manufacturing country. FANUC, Yaskawa, Kawasaki and others build the arms that weld cars, assemble electronics and lift boxes on every continent. These are industrial robots, the workhorses. They don't walk, and they don't chat. They just work.

But here's the strange part. Look at where the robots go. In its latest fiscal year, nearly nine of every ten dollars of FANUC's sales came from customers outside Japan. Its robot sales in China jumped. Its robot sales at home fell. Japan builds the robots. The world buys them.

scenes.narration: So who actually uses the most robots? Count robots per factory worker, and South Korea has nearly three times as many as Japan. China and Germany are ahead of Japan too. The robot superpower is not the most robotic country.

Why would a shortage be good news for robots? Let me draw it. Fewer workers means employers compete for them, so wages rise. Higher wages make a robot look cheap by comparison. So companies buy robots, and every remaining worker produces more. That last box is the whole game. Output per worker. A country can shrink and still get richer per person, if each pair of hands does more.

Step behind the drink fridge in a Tokyo convenience store, and you may find a robot arm sliding cold bottles onto the shelves. Its maker, a startup called Telexistence, says one arm can restock about a thousand drinks a day. When it fumbles a bottle, a person somewhere else puts on a headset and finishes the job remotely. That's not a demo. That's a deployment.

Now compare that with the robots in the headlines. Japan's most famous walking humanoid, Honda's ASIMO, charmed crowds for years and retired without ever getting a real job. Today, Seven-Eleven Japan and Telexistence are developing a humanoid helper, with a target of putting it in stores by twenty twenty-nine. That's a plan, not a product. In Japan, the robots doing the work right now are arms, not androids.

Back at the care home, the helpers are quieter. Sensors under the mattress that tell night staff who is awake. Machines that help lift residents out of bed. Economists who studied Japanese nursing homes found something surprising. Homes that adopted robots ended up with more staff, not fewer, and caregivers spent more of their time on what the researchers call human touch.

Which brings us back to Hiro. One weekend, Aoi comes home with a plan. Not a humanoid. A small collaborative robot arm, the kind built to work safely beside people. They name it Kobo, from the Japanese word for workshop. Aoi writes the program. Kobo loads the lathe, again and again, while Hiro does the part only he can do, checking every piece with a lifetime of experience.

But who gets paid for Kobo? Let me draw it. First, the arm, the hardware. Japan is superb at this. Second, the brain, the AI software that lets a robot see and learn. Much of that is written in America and China. And finally, the user, the small business that puts the robot to work. In an AI economy, more and more of the money flows to the brain and to the user. Japan owns the arm.

keyframes.cue: more and more of the money
keyframes.label: strokes[6].start.cue

scenes.narration: Now the catches. First, the currency. Since the pandemic, Japan's money has lost more than a quarter of its value against the dollar. That makes Japanese robots cheap for foreign buyers, which helps FANUC. But it makes every imported chip, every barrel of fuel and every software subscription more expensive for Hiro.

Second, software. Japan builds superb machines, but the economy around them hasn't kept up. Measured by output per hour worked, Japan sits in the bottom third of the rich-country club. And remember FANUC's robot sales at home? They fell. The robots are being made here. They just aren't spreading fast enough here.

keyframes.cue: The robots are being made here
keyframes.label: items[2].at.cue

scenes.narration: And then there is debt. The IMF says Japan's government owes about twice the size of its entire economy, the highest of any advanced country. The government also owns large financial assets, so the net picture is less extreme. But as more people retire, more money goes to pensions and health care, and there's less room for everything else.

Add it all up, and you can see why so many videos call Japan a slow-motion collapse. Last year, its whole economy grew barely more than one percent. And yet, that headline may be measuring the wrong thing.

Economists led by Jesús Fernández-Villaverde of the University of Pennsylvania asked a different question. Not how fast Japan grew per citizen, but per working-age adult. Their answer? From the late nineties until the pandemic, Japan grew slightly faster than America.

Let me draw it. Japan's total economy looks flat, because the number of workers keeps falling. But divide by the people who actually work, and the line climbs, right alongside America's. Japan's problem was never lazy workers. It was fewer of them. And fewer hands is exactly the problem robots are built to solve.

So, will AI make Japan rich again? Not the way it was in the bubble, when Tokyo land was said to be worth more than entire countries. That boom was built on debt and land prices. This one, if it comes, would be built on output per pair of hands. Robots and AI can let a shrinking Japan keep getting richer per person. But only if small firms like Hiro's actually use them, Japan writes more of the brains and not just the arms, and the debt doesn't crowd everything else out.

In Hoshimachi, the help-wanted sign is still in the window. Hiro still wants an apprentice. But now the parts ship on time, and Aoi comes home to teach Kobo something new. Japan's biggest problem isn't going away. What's changing is what a workshop with too few hands can do.
